co_lakeview.blurb: A small limestone cliff above Vallecito Reservoir, up near 8,000 feet northeast of Durango. Nearly everything here is bolted sport climbing on one pitch, with a single trad line, and the grades cluster in the 5.10s and low 5.11s with a handful of easier routes and a couple of 5.12s. The stone is quite different from the other limestone around Durango and some holds are still coming loose as the wall gets traffic, so a helmet makes sense. The wall faces northwest, so it holds morning shade and takes sun in the afternoon. Catch & Release, Gin & Juiced and Chocolate Covered Razorblades are the routes people tend to climb first. Views over the reservoir are a big part of the draw.
co_lakeview.parking_note: Reach the crag from the Vallecito Reservoir road system: take the county road to the forest road that runs under the dam, pass North Canyon Campground, then turn right onto the short spur that ends near some big boulders. Pull in nose-first so more cars fit.
co_lakeview.approach: A cairned footpath leaves the end of the spur road and climbs past large boulders to the base of the wall in under ten minutes.

co_table_top_area.blurb: A south-facing section of the Golden Cliffs on North Table Mountain, sitting between the Tradlands and the Overhang Area. The cliff is volcanic rock, with short single-pitch lines that mix bolted faces and arêtes with crack and corner routes protected by gear, plus some top-rope setups. Grades run from easy 5.6 and 5.7 up through the 5.10s, with a few harder lines, so it suits a mixed party. Because it faces the sun and sits low, it is a comfortable place on cool and cold days and can get hot in summer; rattlesnakes are around in the warm months. Bolts and anchors here have been replaced in recent years. Climbs are short enough that a standard rope and a modest rack of draws cover most of them.
co_table_top_area.parking_note: Park at one of the trailhead lots serving the Golden Cliffs: either the North Table Mountain Park lot reached from CO 93, or the lots on Peery Parkway, where the lower one should fill first. Drive slowly on the parkway.

co_south_rim_routes.blurb: Long, serious trad climbing on the south side of the Black Canyon of the Gunnison, reached by a drive east of Montrose. These are canyon walls rather than crags: routes run anywhere from a few to well over a dozen pitches, and most grades fall in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with the occasional easier or harder outing. Expect sustained climbing, route-finding puzzles, runouts and rock that needs testing; the canyon is narrow, dark and remote, and getting help is slow, so parties should arrive self-sufficient. Descents can involve multiple rappels or gully scrambling with poison ivy and ticks. Tague Yer Time and Astro Dog are among the more sought-after lines. The south side is generally easier to reach than the opposite rim.

co_mba_buttress.blurb: A short buttress on North Table Mountain just right of the Industrial Buttress, facing roughly southwest. Climbs are a mix of bolted faces, gear-protected cracks and a few boulder problems and top-ropes, with most grades between 5.7 and 5.11. Most of the wall is in the sun, with pockets of shade on hot days, which makes it a good cold-weather pick; wind can blow through on breezy days and rattlesnakes have been seen here in warm months. Shadow of a Hangdog (aka Fat Fingers), Feeding Frenzy and Major Bolt Achievement (MBA) are the standouts. Some anchors can be reached by circling to the top via low-angle breaks, which suits top-roping.

co_wizard_s_gate.blurb: A high, fairly new single-pitch crag on the north side of the Lower Great Face, part of The Crags above the Estes Park Valley near 10,300 feet. The face has tall slabs and a steeply overhanging alcove, and routes are mostly bolted, with a handful of trad lines. Grades span easy 5.8 up to 5.13, with the largest group in the 5.11s and a good number of 5.12s and 5.13s on the overhanging rock. Return of the King offers an easy way in, while Cloak and Dagger, Black Magic and Magic Dagger attract stronger climbers. The slabs stay shaded until late in the day and the alcove never sees sun, so it is best in summer; bring an extra layer, since the altitude feels alpine.
co_wizard_s_gate.parking_note: Drive CO 7 south of Estes Park to the Lily Lake area and park along the dirt road across the highway from the lake, where it ends.
co_wizard_s_gate.approach: Follow the Twin Sisters trail up to roughly the third switchback, then take the faint climber's path north-northeast through trees and boulder fields toward the Central Buttress and around to its north side. It is a steady, steep walk and the path is easy to lose.

co_lion_s_den_the.blurb: A remote moderate bouldering area in the foothills above Lyons, on a small hill covered in boulders. Everything here is bouldering, and most problems fall between V0 and V3, with a smaller group of V4s and a few harder problems up to about V7. Big Cat, Cheeseburger, Hamburger and Hyperion Proboscis are the problems most visitors seek, and the Corridor holds easy warm-ups such as Center Route aka Hall Pass. The setting is quiet and scenic, and the hike keeps crowds down. Some landings are uneven, so bring pads and a spotter.
co_lion_s_den_the.parking_note: From Lyons, drive up US 36 for about four miles, turn left near the cottages, take the road to the left of their driveway, and follow it roughly a mile and a half to a parking lot.
co_lion_s_den_the.approach: A moderately steep trail switchbacks up from the lot, passing a gate and a reservoir, and crosses open woods to the hill of boulders.

co_river_wall_3.blurb: A steep roadside sport wall rising above Clear Creek in the canyon west of Golden. The lower part is slabby and technical, while the upper half steepens into powerful climbing, and almost everything is bolted. Grades are mostly 5.10 to 5.12, with a few easier lines and a single 5.13. River Grill, River Jam, River Dance and White Water are among the routes people repeat. The approach is nearly nothing, but trucks rumble through the nearby tunnel and some routes start above the water, so manage your rope carefully; bring a 60 m rope. The gneiss is reasonably solid, and the wall sees plenty of shade.
co_river_wall_3.parking_note: Pull off on the north side of US 6 about a quarter mile east of Tunnel 2, then walk west toward the bridge; the wall is on the southeast corner of it.
co_river_wall_3.approach: Almost none: most routes start from a wide ledge split by a large boulder, reached from the road by an easy 5.7 or from the river side by a bolted line.

co_whale_the.blurb: A big pink sandstone formation along the west side of Red Rock Canyon Open Space on the edge of Colorado Springs, and one of the park's most popular sport walls. Routes are single-pitch, bolted, up to roughly 130 feet, with lowering anchors, and most grades fall between 5.7 and 5.10, making it a friendly place for newer leaders. Gomers in Blue Shirts is a good 5.10a to try. The stone is soft and crackless, so it can be fragile when damp; give it a few dry days after rain. From the main lot you walk in along the old road and then take the west-side trail to reach the formation. Valuables should not be left in cars here.

co_lower_wall_2.blurb: The ground-level wall of the Puoux, a limestone sport crag beside the highway at the west end of Glenwood Canyon, near Glenwood Springs. Nearly all of the climbs are bolted, with a single trad line and a couple of boulder problems, and most routes start from the ground with almost no approach. Grades range widely, from easy 5.7s through the 5.9s and 5.10s into the low 5.12s, so it suits mixed groups. The stone is sharp and often not yet polished, and quality varies by line. Traffic is generally light. Expect road noise from the interstate, and note that this crag is part of a south- to west-facing system.
co_lower_wall_2.parking_note: Use the large pull-out on the roadside about 300 feet east of the Glenwood Springs tunnel; the crag is visible from the pavement.
